title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation
description: Brute force to optimized: eagerly updating up to k elements versus a lazy propagation trick that resolves the update incrementally as elements are popped.

sections.title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation

content.title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a stack that supports the following operations: CustomStack(int maxSize) initializes with a maximum capacity; push(x) adds x if the stack has not reached maxSize; pop() removes and returns the top element (or -1 if empty); increment(k, val) increments the BOTTOM min(k, current size) elements of the stack by val.

blocks.caption: increment only ever touches the bottom-most elements of the stack, which suggests a lazy, deferred-update trick rather than eagerly updating every affected element

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of push/pop/increment operations, plus a maxSize"],["Output","For each pop call, the returned value"],["Goal","Support push and pop in O(1), and ideally increment in O(1) as well (rather than O(k))"],["Constraints","1 <= maxSize <= 1000; 1 <= x, val <= 1000; 0 <= k <= 1000; at most 1000 calls total to push, pop, and increment"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["increment always affects a CONTIGUOUS range starting from the BOTTOM","A \"lazy propagation\" trick: instead of updating every affected element immediately, record a single pending adjustment and only resolve it when an element is actually popped"],["Elements are always removed from the TOP (standard stack order)","A pending increment recorded near the top of the affected range can be \"pushed down\" to the next element below it as each pop happens, keeping every future pop still correct"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

push and pop behave like a standard array-backed stack; increment(k, val) is the interesting operation, since naively applying it would require touching up to k elements individually, even though most of those elements might not be popped again for a long time (or ever, if more pushes happen first).

blocks.title: Analogy: A Stack of Trays With a "Pending Bonus" Sticky Note
blocks.text: Imagine a cafeteria tray stack where, instead of physically re-labeling every tray in a range with a bonus point value (slow if there are many trays), a single sticky note is placed on the TOPMOST tray of that range, saying "+100 to me and everyone below me in this range." When a tray is actually taken (popped) from the top, its own sticky note bonus is applied immediately, and if there IS a sticky note still on it, that bonus is passed DOWN to the tray now newly exposed on top, so the pending bonus is never lost, just deferred.

blocks.caption: A pending increment recorded at ONE position gets pushed down to the next position as each pop resolves it, deferring the O(k) cost until elements are actually popped

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: maxSize=3; push(1), push(2), pop(), push(2), push(3), push(4) (rejected, full), increment(5,100), increment(2,100), pop(), pop(), pop(), pop()

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before eagerly updating every one of the k affected elements on each increment call (potentially O(k) per call, repeated many times), notice that increment ALWAYS affects a range starting from the bottom, which suggests deferring the actual update until an element is popped, using a single "pending adjustment" marker.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: increment(k, val) always affects elements starting from INDEX 0 (the bottom) up to index min(k, size) - 1; the TOPMOST element within that range is index min(k, size) - 1.

Observation 2: Instead of adding val to all min(k, size) elements immediately, a single "pending increment" can be recorded AT that topmost affected index, representing "this element, and everything below it, still owes +val."

Observation 3: When pop() removes the current top element, that element's own pending increment (if any) is applied to it right then; crucially, that same pending amount must then be TRANSFERRED down to the element now newly exposed as the top (added to whatever pending increment IT already has), so the deferred amount is never lost for the remaining elements.

Observation 4: This "push the pending amount down by exactly one position on every pop" trick ensures every element eventually receives its correctly accumulated total increment, exactly once, right when it is actually popped, never needing to eagerly touch elements that might not be popped again for a long time.

This is a lazy propagation technique: increment records a single pending adjustment at the top of the affected range, and each pop resolves (and forwards) that pending amount, achieving O(1) for every operation.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a plain array-backed stack; for increment(k, val), directly walk and update each of the bottom min(k, size) elements.
Step by step algorithm

items: push and pop operate directly on a plain array/list, in O(1).
increment(k, val) loops through the bottom min(k, size) elements, adding val to each one individually.

codes.python:
class CustomStack:
    def __init__(self, max_size):
        self.max_size = max_size
        self.stack = []

    def push(self, x):
        if len(self.stack) < self.max_size:
            self.stack.append(x)

    def pop(self):
        return self.stack.pop() if self.stack else -1

    def increment(self, k, val):
        for i in range(min(k, len(self.stack))):                           # walk the bottom min(k, size) elements one at a time
            self.stack[i] += val


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cs = CustomStack(3)
    cs.push(1)
    cs.push(2)
    print(cs.pop())
    cs.push(2)
    cs.push(3)
    cs.push(4)
    cs.increment(5, 100)
    cs.increment(2, 100)
    print(cs.pop())
    print(cs.pop())
    print(cs.pop())
    print(cs.pop())

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: push and pop are already optimal using a plain array; no changes needed there.
increment directly and simply applies the definition, touching every affected element immediately, correctly but at O(k) cost per call.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly applies every increment immediately, since it directly touches exactly the elements the definition specifies.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for push/pop, but O(k) for each increment call.
Space: O(maxSize).

Limitation: given up to 1000 increment calls each potentially touching up to 1000 elements, the total work can reach O(n^2) in the worst case; deferring the update via lazy propagation achieves O(1) for every single operation.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force eagerly touches up to k elements on every increment call. Instead, maintain a parallel "increments" array; increment(k, val) records val at ONLY the topmost affected index (min(k, size) - 1), representing a pending adjustment for that element AND everything below it. On pop(), apply the popped element's own pending increment to its returned value, then transfer that same pending amount down to the new top (adding it to whatever pending increment is already there), so it is never lost for the remaining elements.

Maintain a stack array and a parallel increments array (both same size, or growing together). push(x): append x and a 0 pending increment. pop(): remove the top value and its pending increment, add them together as the return value; if any elements remain, add this popped pending increment to the new top's own pending increment. increment(k, val): if the stack is non-empty, add val to increments[min(k, size) - 1] only.
9. Optimized Solution
Use a lazy propagation technique: increment records a single pending adjustment at the top of the affected range; each pop resolves and forwards that pending amount.
Dry run for stack=[1,2,3] (after the setup push/pop cycle), increment(5,100), increment(2,100), then 4 pops

codes.python:
class CustomStack:
    def __init__(self, max_size):
        self.max_size = max_size
        self.stack = []
        self.increments = []                                               # increments[i] = a PENDING increment for the element at position i

    def push(self, x):
        if len(self.stack) < self.max_size:
            self.stack.append(x)
            self.increments.append(0)                                     # every new element starts with no pending increment

    def pop(self):
        if not self.stack:
            return -1
        pending = self.increments.pop()                                    # this element's own pending increment
        val = self.stack.pop() + pending                                   # apply it, right when the element is actually popped
        if self.increments:
            self.increments[-1] += pending                                 # push the pending increment DOWN to the new top, so it isn't lost
        return val

    def increment(self, k, val):
        if self.stack:
            idx = min(k, len(self.stack)) - 1                               # only record the increment at ONE position: the top of the affected range
            self.increments[idx] += val


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cs = CustomStack(3)
    cs.push(1)
    cs.push(2)
    print(cs.pop())
    cs.push(2)
    cs.push(3)
    cs.push(4)
    cs.increment(5, 100)
    cs.increment(2, 100)
    print(cs.pop())
    print(cs.pop())
    print(cs.pop())
    print(cs.pop())

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for push, pop, AND increment.
Space: O(maxSize), for the stack and its parallel increments array.
Why This Works

Recording a pending increment at ONLY the topmost affected index is sufficient, because that pending amount is guaranteed to be "passed down" to whatever becomes the new top on every subsequent pop, exactly propagating the intended effect to every element in the original range, one pop at a time, without ever needing to eagerly touch elements that might not be popped for a while.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["increment(k, val) is called","Only ONE array position (the topmost affected index) is updated: O(1)"],["pop() removes an element with a pending increment","That amount is applied to the returned value, then transferred down to the new top's own pending increment"],["Multiple increment calls affect overlapping ranges","Their pending amounts simply accumulate (via addition) at whichever positions they each individually target"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The increments array is always the SAME size as the stack, growing and shrinking together with push and pop.

On pop, the ORDER matters: first compute the return value using the popped element's OWN pending increment, THEN transfer that same pending amount down to the new top, before clearing the popped position's now-unused increment slot.
increment only ever writes to ONE position (never loops), which is the key change from the brute force's O(k) loop.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (eager per-element increment)","O(1) push/pop, O(k) increment","O(maxSize)","Directly touches every affected element on each increment call"],["Optimized (lazy propagation via a single pending marker)","O(1) for every operation","O(maxSize)","Defers the update, resolving it incrementally as elements are actually popped"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When an operation needs to affect a RANGE that always starts from one fixed end (here, the stack's bottom), and elements are only ever removed from the OTHER end (the top), a lazy propagation trick, recording a single pending adjustment and resolving it incrementally as elements are removed, can turn an O(k)-per-call operation into O(1).
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to TRANSFER the popped element's pending increment down to the new top, which would silently lose that pending amount for all remaining elements.
Recording the pending increment at the WRONG index (not the topmost affected position, min(k, size) - 1).
Applying the SAME pending increment twice (once when popped, and again when incorrectly not cleared afterward).

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["increment called on an empty stack","Does nothing, since there is nothing to increment"],["k larger than the current stack size","Correctly capped at min(k, size), affecting only the elements that actually exist"],["pop called on an empty stack","Returns -1, per the problem's specification"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly explaining the "defer the work, resolve it on pop, transfer the remainder down" mechanism (rather than just describing WHAT is stored) demonstrates a clear understanding of exactly why the lazy technique achieves O(1) amortized correctness.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "A range update ALWAYS starts from one fixed end, and removal happens from the OTHER end" points toward lazy propagation: defer the update, resolving and forwarding it incrementally as elements are removed.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does this differ from a Fenwick tree's lazy range-update technique? Both defer work using a similar "record at one point, resolve incrementally" idea, though a Fenwick tree generalizes this to arbitrary range queries, not just a fixed bottom-to-variable-top pattern.

What would change if increment could also affect a range NOT starting from the bottom? The single-marker trick relies specifically on the range always starting from a fixed end; a more general range-update structure (like a difference array or segment tree) would be needed otherwise.

How would you verify the transfer-down logic is correct? Trace an example with MULTIPLE overlapping increment calls before any pops occur, confirming each element's final popped value correctly reflects the SUM of every increment call that should have affected it.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A lazy propagation / deferred-update technique conceptually related to difference arrays and segment tree lazy propagation, here specialized for a stack whose range updates always anchor to one fixed end.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) push/pop, O(k) increment; O(maxSize) space.
Optimized (lazy propagation): O(1) for every operation; O(maxSize) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Lazy propagation via a single pending-adjustment marker
Core Idea: increment records a pending amount at only the topmost affected index; each pop applies (and forwards down) that element's pending increment, resolving the deferred work incrementally
Time: O(1) for every operation
Space: O(maxSize)
Most Important Observation: A pending increment must be TRANSFERRED down to the new top on every pop, or it would be permanently lost for the remaining elements
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: increment: add val to increments[min(k,size)-1] only. pop: apply own increment, then push it down to the new top
